links.note: Martin Luther printed the Theologia Deutsch at Wittenberg, part of it in 1516 and a fuller text in 1518. In his preface he wrote that, next to the Bible and Augustine, no book had taught him more of God, Christ and man. In 1521 he cited Tauler on purgatory.
links.outcome_considered: Luther printed and praised the book, which shows a text taken up by the other side; no source on this link shows a council, a split or a changed rule.

links.note: Johannes Busch kept the chronicle of the Windesheim canons. He tells how their prior, at the council of Constance, gladly visited the cell of the friar who wrote the Clock of Eternal Wisdom. The chronicle's 1886 editor names that friar as Henry Suso. A 1902 editor of Thomas a Kempis lists Suso among the writers Thomas took sayings from.
links.outcome_considered: The sources show reverence for Suso and borrowing from his books, not a council, a split or a changed rule.

links.note: Johannes Busch, a canon of Windesheim, wrote that his brother canon Thomas a Kempis made the Imitation of Christ. Ignatius of Loyola's Spiritual Exercises tell those who make them to read it from the second week on. A Jesuit who knew Ignatius said he kept just two books on his table: the New Testament and Thomas a Kempis.
links.outcome_considered: The sources show the Imitation set as reading and kept by Ignatius, a text taken up by the other side; that does not meet the test.

links.note: In 1629 Augustine Baker, an English monk at Cambrai, wrote a guide to The Cloud of Unknowing for the English nuns there. He said his copy came from one that English Carthusians took abroad when they left England under Henry VIII. In 1670 Serenus Cressy, who had become a monk with the English at Douai, printed Julian's book.
links.outcome_considered: The sources show the books copied, explained and printed by English Catholics abroad, a text taken up by the other side; that does not meet the test.

links.note: In December 1367 at Erfurt, a beghard called John Hartmann was questioned by Walter Kerling, named by the pope's authority to try heresy. Kerling put to him the first article of Ad nostrum, a decree of the Council of Vienne. In 1887 Wilhelm Wattenbach noted that the questions kept to the decree point by point. He added that such answers were often forced.
links.outcome: The Council of Vienne condemned errors it laid on beguines and beghards. In 1367 a papal inquisitor still put that decree to a suspect, point by point.

dispositions.sentence: Across a single century a scattering of English men and women began writing about the inner life of prayer in their own language rather than in Latin — Richard Rolle the Yorkshire hermit with his Fire of Love, Walter Hilton with the Scale of Perfection, and the anonymous author of The Cloud of Unknowing, all writing for recluses and devout lay people rather than for scholars.
dispositions.reason: Names the movement's own writers and readers; no tie to another movement.

dispositions.sentence: Julian of Norwich, an anchoress enclosed in a cell beside a Norwich parish church, spent decades revising an account of sixteen revelations she had received during a near-fatal illness, arriving at the line she is still known for: that all shall be well.

prose_changes.old: Across a single century a scattering of English men and women began writing about the inner life of prayer in their own language rather than in Latin — Richard Rolle the Yorkshire hermit with his Fire of Love, Walter Hilton with the Scale of Perfection, and the anonymous author of The Cloud of Unknowing, all writing for recluses and devout lay people rather than for scholars.
